summary: Comments from Vint Cerf that review and expand on the mail transition plan. It discusses how to keep mail, the most heavily used network service, working while moving from ARPANET protocols to Internet protocols, with the least disruption to users and software.

plainLanguage.summary: When a town changes road systems, someone has to make sure the mail trucks still get through. This memo adds notes on how to keep email flowing during the switch.

subtitle: Comments and detailed guidance on managing email during the protocol transition.

tldr.problem: The transition from NCP-based mail to TCP-based mail is complex, with a mix of old and new hosts. The plan needs clarification and detailed implementation strategy, particularly for implicit versus explicit forwarding of mail.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes two forwarding approaches: explicit forwarders (for hosts that know to use them) and implicit forwarders (for old NCP hosts that do not know the destination is TCP-only). Implicit forwarders hold a registry of TCP mailbox names mapped from their host names.
tldr.outcome: By distinguishing implicit and explicit forwarding and managing mailbox registries, the transition can accommodate old hosts without changes, while allowing new hosts to reach TCP destinations.

today: RFC 773 comments are now purely historical. The Internet transition was completed by 1983, and ARPANET protocols were entirely superseded. Modern email uses SMTP over TCP exclusively.

sections.title: The Transition Goals
sections.content:
This memo reviews and expands on the transition plan. The principal aim is to support the most heavily used network service (electronic mail) during the transition from ARPANET to Internet protocols. The five ground rules are: (1) ARPANET mailbox names must continue to work, (2) no changes to mail editors parsing headers, (3) non-ARPANET names must be accommodated without change to mail composition, (4) automatic forwarding without user intervention, and (5) old mail mechanisms must still work.

The memo addresses only text mail, not future transitions to multimedia mail.
sections.plainLanguage: Email must keep working during the switch. Old addresses must still work. People should not have to change their email programs.

sections.title: Implicit and Explicit Forwarding
sections.content:
Explicit forwarders are used by hosts that have adopted the new Internet tables: a host can tell whether the destination is NCP or TCP and explicitly sends to an intermediate forwarder if needed. Implicit forwarders are used for old NCP hosts with no changes except an extended host table. When an old host sends to what it thinks is an NCP destination, it actually sends to an implicit forwarder that has a registry of TCP mailbox names.

The challenge is that old FTP mail commands only send the mailbox name, not the host. An implicit forwarder must look up the mailbox in its registry to find the real destination host. Internet mailbox users must register themselves at implicit forwarders so old systems can reach them; this is the price of compatibility with unchanged old hosts.
sections.plainLanguage: If a new host knows about the transition, it can pick the right forwarding route. If an old host does not know, it sends to a special post office that has a phone book of who went where.

sections.title: Host Types and Communication Patterns
sections.content:
Three host types are defined: unchanged old NCP (RFC 733 only), NCP with new Internet tables, and TCP with new Internet tables. Each pair of host types has a communication pattern. The three-by-three matrix shows that: old NCP to new TCP requires implicit forwarding with registry lookup, new NCP to TCP requires explicit forwarding, and TCP to NCP requires explicit forwarding to a relay.

Mail composition programs (SNDMSG, MSG, Hermes, MH, etc.) can continue using old tables as long as they are updated to include Internet host names alongside ARPANET names. In the hardest case (old NCP to new TCP), implicit forwarding is transparent to the old host and its applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Different types of hosts have different rules. The system is designed so an old host does not have to learn the new rules; a relay does the translation for it.

sections.title: Implementation Schedule and Challenges
sections.content: The proposed schedule is: January 1981 introduce implicit and explicit forwarders, January 1982 remove implicit forwarding service, January 1983 complete transition to TCP. Key challenges remain to be worked out: error message handling via forwarders, designation of which hosts act as forwarders, collection and distribution of Internet mailbox registries at implicit forwarders, format and distribution of the Internet name tables and capability information, and handling of mail systems incompatible with NCP, TCP, or RFC 733 (Telemail, On-Tyme, TWX, TELEX, etc.).
sections.plainLanguage: The plan sets a three-year timeline. There are still details to figure out, like how to handle errors and how to keep everyone's address books in sync.
